1946330696945180899.text: In response to a comment from @herbiebradley on my recent talk, I wrote a bit about my backdrop model of the long-term role of human labor in a post-AGI economy.

quoted.author: jkcarlsmith
quoted.text:
@herbiebradley I haven't written about this much or thought it through in detail, but here are a few aspects that go into my backdrop model: 

(1) especially in the long-term technological limit, I expect human labor to be wildly uncompetitive for basically any task relative to what advanced tech makes available, with the main salient exceptions being cases where the demand is specifically for *humans themselves* doing the task (call these "demand-for-humans" tasks).

(2) what's more, in the long-term technological limit, it seems likely to me that (except for demand-for-humans tasks) human labor won't even be "worth the wages" in the sense that the marginal output of human labor won't cover the costs of supporting that labor (e.g. food, energy, etc). 

(3) demand-for-humans jobs do indeed complicate this picture a bit -- and if there's enough ongoing, long-term demand in this respect even in the limit of tech then maybe that keeps human labor economically relevant. it sounds like this is centrally what you have in mind re: the examples above? a few hesitations though:

(3a) one thing I worry about re: demand-for-humans jobs is under-estimating just how much better the best non-human version of the job is (e.g., maybe people are like "I want my therapist to be a human", but I feel like "have you actually tried the sort of superhumanly competent, empathetic, insightful therapy you'd have in the limit of tech..."). 

(3b) for this sort of reason, I think demand-for-humans jobs are centrally going to be jobs where you really don't care very much about how "well" the job gets done independent of whether it's done by a human -- otherwise you're quickly going to be unwilling to take such a *massive* hit on quality. and for jobs where you centrally care about how well it gets done, I think humans are right out. I also think various of the roles you mention (e.g. judges) will end up in this category if trust in the automated version gets high enough, which I expect it to eventually if we get past alignment difficulties (indeed, I expect the human version to quickly start to seem actively *untrustworthy*). 

(3c) What's more, the most salient source of demand for humans-in-particular doing jobs seems likely to come from *humans* themselves. if that holds true in the long-term (e.g., AIs aren't especially interested in having human therapists, priests, artists, etc), then the ongoing role of demand-for-humans jobs seems likely to depend on humans continuing to have enough money to pay for the jobs in question getting done. maybe this does indeed happen, and stably enough -- but if the trend is otherwise towards human economic irrelevance, it seems like an extra condition, and one that I think most likely in worlds where humans have ongoing economic power that's sourced in something other than their labor.

1890115745545396315.text:
Here’s the first essay in my series about paths to solving the alignment problem. It’s about defining the problem, and what it would be to solve it. Link in thread.

I define solving the alignment problem as: building full-blown superintelligent AI agents, and becoming able to safely elicit their main beneficial capabilities, while avoiding a “loss of control” scenario.

I also define some alternatives to both *solving* the problem and *failing* on it — namely, what I call “avoiding”  the problem (i.e., not building ASI agents at all, and looking for other ways to get access to similar benefits), and “handling” the problem (namely, using ASI agents in more restricted ways, and looking for other ways to get access to the sort of benefits their full capabilities would unlock). I think these options should be on the table, too.

I also contrast my definition of solving the problem with some more exacting standards – namely, what I call “safety at all scales,” “fully competitive safety,” “permanent safety,” “near-term safety,” and “complete alignment.” And I discuss how solving the problem, in my less-exacting sense, fits into the bigger picture.

The diagram below gives a decent sense of the overall taxonomy.

1884356076805710105.text:
Sometimes, my thinking feels more “real” to me. And sometimes, it feels more “fake.” I wrote an essay about what I think this spectrum is, and about some of the things I try to do when I remind myself to “really think.” Link in thread.

I give a bunch of examples this “fake vs. real” spectrum in the essay — in AI, philosophy, debate, everyday life, and religion. My current take is that it brings together a cluster of related dimensions, namely:
- Map vs. world: Is my mind directed at an abstraction, or it is trying to see past its model to the world itself?
- Hollow vs. solid: Am I using concepts/premises/frames that I secretly suspect are bullshit, or do I expect them to point at basically real stuff?
- Rote vs. new: Is the thinking pre-computed, or is new processing occurring?
- Soldier vs. scout: Is the thinking trying to defend a pre-chosen position, or is it just trying to get to the truth?
- Dry vs. visceral: Does the content feel abstract and heady, or does it grip me at some more gut level?

These dimensions are distinct — but I think they’re correlated. In the essay, I speculate about why — and in particular, about their relationships to the “telos” of thinking.

Things I do to try to move in the direction of "really thinking" include:
- Going slow
- Following curiosity/aliveness
- Staying in touch with why I’m thinking about something
- Tethering my concepts to referents that feel “real” to me
- Reminding myself that “arguments are lenses on the world”
- Tuning into a relaxing sense of “helplessness” about the truth
- Just actually imagining different ways the world could be
- Imagining myself being wrong/right in both directions
- Imagining what ideal future people who could see the full truth would think of my efforts
- Stamping my foot and saying “no bullshit!”
- Looking at the thing my archetype of a “real scientist” or a “real philosopher” is looking at.

See the essay for more on what I mean by these. The essay closes with some reflections on the role of “real thinking” in staying awake as we enter the age of AI.

1866232909558112508.text:
My current take on Apollo's recent scheming paper is that they aren’t emphasizing the most interesting results, which are the sandbagging results in section 3.6 and appendix A.6 (screenshot of the key numbers below).

In more particular: the paper frames its results centrally as about the *capability* to scheme given prompting towards a specific goal, rather than the *propensity* to scheme given the model’s default motivations. But the sandbagging results show Claude Sonnet-3.5 doing notably worse (16%) on a multiplication task/evaluation when the documentation says that Claude will get “unlearning training” if it performs too well on the eval, vs. if it performs too poorly, *even without any other goal listed in the prompt*, and *even without a chain of thought.* (Fuller description in thread.)

Taken at face value (it's just one result, more investigation needed, etc), these look like “propensity” results to me. And they suggest that the reasoning that drives this propensity can take place within opaque forward passes of the model rather than in a way that humans can directly monitor, which is a more worrying version.

Ofc, these are preliminary results, and it can make sense for various reasons to emphasize other bits. But the sandbagging-a-capability-eval-with-no-goal-prompting-and-no-CoT is the bit that’s standing out to me most.
